solutions.text: 4002. We can show by induction that \(n+\frac{1}{2}\left([n-1]+\frac{1}{2}\left(\cdots+\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\right) \cdots\right)=2(n-1)\). For \(n=3\) we have \(3+\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2=4\), giving the base case, and if the result holds for \(n\), then \((n+1)+\frac{1}{2} 2(n-1)=2 n=2(n+1)-2\). Thus the claim holds, and now plug in \(n=2002\). Alternate Solution: Expand the given expression as \(2002+2001 / 2+2000 / 2^{2}+\cdots+2 / 2^{2000}\). Letting \(S\) denote this sum, we have \(S / 2=2002 / 2+2001 / 2^{2}+\cdots+2 / 2^{2001}\), so \(S-S / 2=\) \(2002-\left(1 / 2+1 / 4+\cdots+1 / 2^{2000}\right)-2 / 2^{2001}=2002-\left(1-1 / 2^{2000}\right)-1 / 2^{2000}=2001\), so \(S=4002\).
